hints.junior: Polling the DOM on a timer means most checks find nothing, and the one check that matters can still be up to your polling interval late.
hints.mid: A setInterval poll loop keeps running forever, even long after the change you were waiting for already happened.
hints.staff: MutationObserver batches its notifications into microtasks, so rapid DOM changes in the same tick arrive as one array of records, not one callback per change.

hints.junior: Watch the check counter in polling mode climb the whole time, even after the target element already appeared. Observer mode fires exactly once, right when it happens.
hints.mid: The polling version keeps querying the DOM every 100ms indefinitely; the observer version does zero work until the actual mutation occurs.
hints.staff: Compare the total query count between modes after the same simulated delay — polling mode's count scales with wait time, observer mode's doesn't.

hints.junior: MutationObserver watches for a change and calls your function the moment it happens, instead of you repeatedly asking whether it happened yet.
hints.mid: You create an observer with a callback, then call observe() on a target node with a config describing what to watch: child list, attributes, or text changes.
hints.staff: The browser delivers mutation records as a batched array per microtask, which is part of why observers stay cheap even on busy pages.

hints.junior: Watch as narrow a part of the page as you can, and only set subtree true if you actually need to see changes in descendant elements too.
hints.mid: Call observer.disconnect() once you've gotten the change you needed, or in a cleanup function — don't leave it running for the page's whole lifetime.
hints.staff: For high-frequency mutation sources, iterate the whole records array once per callback rather than reacting per individual mutation record.

sections.junior: Hey! Today we're replacing a setInterval poll loop with something that actually tells you the moment a DOM change happens.
sections.mid: This case covers MutationObserver as the precise, zero-waste alternative to polling the DOM on a timer.
sections.staff: We're covering observer scoping, microtask batching of mutation records, and when to disconnect an observer.

sections.junior: MutationObserver watches for a change and calls your function the instant it happens, instead of you repeatedly checking.
sections.mid: You configure what to watch, child list, attributes, or text, and the browser calls you back exactly when a matching change occurs.
sections.staff: Mutation records arrive batched per microtask, so many rapid changes in one tick still produce a single callback invocation.

sections.junior: Watch the check counter in polling mode keep climbing forever. The observer mode counter only moves once, right when the change happens.
sections.mid: Polling keeps querying on a fixed interval regardless of whether anything changed; the observer does zero work until a real mutation occurs.
sections.staff: Compare total query counts between modes over the same wait duration to see the difference directly.

sections.junior: Don't poll the DOM on a timer for a change you're waiting for. MutationObserver tells you the moment it happens.
sections.mid: Scope the observer as narrowly as possible, and disconnect it once you’ve gotten what you needed.
sections.staff: Mutation callbacks are batched into microtasks and deliver an array of records, so handle them in one pass rather than reacting per mutation.
